summary: Root cause identified with medium confidence (0.72): the pricing-engine config ramp cfg-3120 (flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5→100 at 12:04Z) turned on the expensive GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator (20000 paths, 6.5–8.4s per call) for all traffic, pinning pricing-engine CPU at ~99% and driving p99 from ~60ms to ~2535ms — far beyond its own 2000ms quote budget — so order-service's 2500ms client calls timed out. The onset is strictly one minute after the ramp (CPU 38–42% through 12:04Z → 98.65% at 12:05Z; p99 56.8–63.1ms → 2534.9ms) with zero precursor, and capacity loss is excluded (flat request_rate, 0 restarts, flat memory). The competing hypotheses are contradicted by direct telemetry: market-data-service's 11:56Z protobuf deploy shows flat p99/error_rate and pricing-engine was unaffected for 8+ minutes after it, and redis-cache metrics are flat. No revert of the flag has occurred, so the decisive recovery-on-revert confirmation is absent, but the flag ramp is the only change in the window and the causal chain is temporally tight.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Greeks v2 flag ramp to 100% saturates pricing-engine CPU → quote budget exceeded → order-service timeouts
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A config change on pricing-engine (flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5→100 at 12:04Z, cfg-3120) turned on the expensive GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator for essentially all traffic. The 20000-path Monte-Carlo computation (6.5-8.4s per call) pinned pricing-engine CPU at ~99% and drove p99 from ~60ms to ~2528ms, so pricing-engine blew its own 2000ms quote budget and returned too slowly for order-service's 2500ms client timeout, producing the reported quote timeouts. The new 1-minute-resolution data (F25-F30) resolves the critic's central objection: the onset is strictly at 12:05Z with zero precursor, exactly one minute after the flag ramp, while capacity proxies (request_rate, restarts, memory) are unchanged.

causal_chain.claim: Config change cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 on pricing-engine at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z; it is the only change on any service inside the incident window and the only pricing-engine change in [11:00Z,13:59Z] (no revert, no rollback)
GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo (paths=20000) becomes active for ~all traffic at the ramp; first WARN at 12:05:21Z, zero WARNs anywhere in 11:50-12:05Z
pricing-engine CPU steps from a flat 38-42% baseline (every 1-min bucket 11:50-12:04Z) to 98.65% at 12:05Z and 99.25-100% thereafter
pricing-engine p99 steps from 56.8-63.1ms in every bucket 11:50-12:04Z to 2534.9ms at 12:05Z, sustained 2500-2850ms through 13:56Z
pricing-engine CPU/latency/WARN steps are NOT caused by capacity loss: request_rate flat 590-687 req/s with no drop at onset, restarts 0.0 every bucket, memory_pct flat 46-53%
pricing-engine exceeds its own 2000ms quote budget ('request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2'), first ERROR 12:06:41Z

order-service calls time out client-side at 2500ms ('pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms'), first ERROR 12:06:10Z, error_rate plateauing ~8.1-8.4%; order-service CPU flat ~40% with no step, so it is a victim not origin
Time-ordered chain: ramp 12:04Z → CPU/latency step 12:05Z → GreeksV2 WARN 12:05:21Z → order-service timeout 12:06:10Z, with no precursor in 11:50-12:04Z

assumptions: Algorithmic Monte-Carlo cost is the CPU driver rather than a simultaneous capacity reduction. Strongly supported indirectly (F28: flat request_rate, 0 restarts, flat memory) but not directly proven because pricing-engine exposes no replica_count metric and has no deployment object.

The flag was never reverted or rolled back; no recovery is observed through 13:59Z. Thus the decisive 'recovers on revert' confirmation is absent — it could not be obtained because no revert ever happened (F31, F33).

order-service's 2500ms client timeout is longer than pricing-engine's 2000ms budget, so slow-but-not-failed pricing-engine calls translate into client timeouts. Consistent with the uniform timeout signature (F7), though the exact interplay is inferred.

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization change (v5.2.0) breaks the quote path and cascades into order-service timeouts
ranked_hypotheses.statement: market-data-service v5.2.0 ('Switch quote serialization to protobuf') changed the quote payload format at 11:56Z. Pricing-engine consumes market-data-service over HTTP on the quote path; the new/malformed payload could force expensive or pathological handling in pricing-engine, driving CPU/latency up and cascading into order-service timeouts. This is now directly contradicted: market-data-service itself shows no latency or error step at or after its own deploy, and the pricing-engine onset is 8-9 minutes after the deploy and exactly aligned with the later flag ramp instead.

causal_chain.claim: market-data-service v5.2.0 ships protobuf quote payloads at 11:56Z; it is the only deployment on any service in [11:00Z,13:59Z] and was never rolled back
pricing-engine consumes market-data-service on the quote path (pricing-engine -> market-data-service http)
The new payload format triggers costly/degraded handling inside pricing-engine
pricing-engine CPU/latency step and order-service timeouts follow

assumptions: A protobuf serialization change would manifest as CPU-bound Monte-Carlo computation — unverified and mechanistically implausible.

The ~8-10 minute gap between the deploy and onset reflects a slow-burn payload effect rather than coincidence; but pricing-engine was rock-steady (38-42% CPU, 57-63ms p99) throughout that entire 8-9 minute gap.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct telemetry now contradicts this. market-data-service latency_p99 stayed 36.5-42.3ms across all 26 buckets 11:50-12:15Z with no step at its own 11:56Z deploy (F21); its error_rate stayed flat 0.11-0.32% (F22). Critically, pricing-engine was completely unaffected for the entire 8-9 minutes after the deploy — flat 38-42% CPU and 57-63ms p99 in every 1-min bucket 11:50-12:04Z — then stepped at 12:05Z, one minute after the unrelated flag ramp (F25, F26). A payload effect with zero signal for 8 minutes and none at the origin service is not credible. HIST-107 is a cache-miss precedent, not a serialization one (F18).

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation throttles the pricing-engine/market-data-service quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache is shared by both pricing-engine and market-data-service and is a platform-owned component on order-service's depth-2 quote path. A redis-cache degradation could slow pricing-engine's quote computation, inflating latency and cascading into order-service timeouts independent of any service's own change. This is now directly contradicted by telemetry: redis-cache hit ratio, CPU, connected clients and evictions are all flat and healthy across the window with no step at either the 11:56Z deploy or the 12:04Z ramp.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache is shared by pricing-engine and market-data-service and sits on order-service's depth-2 quote path
redis-cache degrades (hit-rate collapse / latency rise / connection saturatoin)
pricing-engine quote computation slows and CPU contention rises
order-service quote calls exceed the 2500ms client timeout

assumptions: A redis degradation large enough to pin GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo compute at 99% CPU would be required, but no redis anomaly exists to trigger it.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct telemetry now contradicts this. redis-cache hit ratio was flat and healthy (93.83%-98.46%, mean 96.25) with no step at the 11:56Z deploy or 12:04Z ramp (F19); CPU 20.7-23.2%, connected_clients 288-335, evictions 2.15-3.76/min, none stepping (F20). The failure mechanism (CPU-bound internal Monte-Carlo compute) also does not match a cache degradation (F17, F24). The critic's objection (zero redis metrics retrieved) has been addressed.

ranked_hypotheses.title: order-service self-degradation (retry storm / connection-pool exhaustion) is the primary fault, pricing-engine p99 is downstream
ranked_hypotheses.statement: order-service's own degradation is the origin: it saturates its own resources (retry storms, connection-pool exhaustion) and in doing so inflates load on pricing-engine, whose p99 of 2.6s is a downstream symptom. order-service timeouts are the primary fault.

causal_chain.claim: order-service begins failing/retrying at the quote step
Its resource usage or retry volume saturates
Extra load degrades pricing-engine, producing its p99/latency jump

assumptions: Pricing-engine's CPU saturation would have to be caused by order-service traffic.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: order-service CPU stayed flat at ~40% (max 44.24) with no step at onset (F12); pricing-engine CPU/latency step at 12:05Z follows the pricing-engine GreeksV2 flag ramp at 12:04Z (F15, F25, F26), not any order-service action. pricing-engine's own GreeksV2 WARNs (12:05:21Z) precede order-service's first ERROR (12:06:10Z), so pricing-engine degrades first (F8, F27, F29). Request_rate on pricing-engine was flat, so no load influx (F28).

facts.statement: A config change on pricing-engine, flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5→100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'), is the only change on any service within the incident window.

pricing-engine latency_p99 was 56.82–63.09ms in every 1-minute bucket 11:50Z–12:04Z inclusive and jumped to 2534.9ms at 12:05Z (max 2849.25 later), staying 2500–2850ms through 13:56.

Capacity loss is excluded as the CPU driver: pricing-engine request_rate is flat 590.66–687.48 req/s across 11:50Z–12:10Z with no drop at onset, restarts are 0.0 in every bucket, and memory_pct stays 46.04–52.78%.
order-service error_rate rose from a 0.17–0.25% baseline to 6.08% in the 12:04:00 bucket and plateaued at ~8.1–8.4% through 13:56 (max 8.87), matching sustained pricing-engine saturation.

order-service CPU stayed flat at ~40% (max 44.24) across 11:00–13:56 with no step at onset, so its degradation is not CPU-driven and is consistent with downstream timeouts; order-service had zero deployments in [11:00Z,13:59Z].
redis-cache shows no degradation: hit ratio 93.83–98.46% (mean 96.25), cpu_pct 20.73–23.17, connected_clients 288.17–335.37, evictions_per_min 2.15–3.76 — none stepping at 11:56Z or 12:04Z.

pricing-engine WARN/ERROR logs 12:00–12:10Z contain only GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo and deadline-exceeded signatures; no protobuf/deserialization/parse/schema-mismatch message appears among the 23 returned entries.

The only deployment across all services in [11:00Z,13:59Z] is market-data-service v5.2.0 at 11:56:00Z ('Switch quote serialization to protobuf', rolled_back_at null), which precedes the causal-side onset by ~8–10 minutes, not 'a few minutes'.

The all-services config-change re-run for [12:00Z,13:59Z] returns count 1 with partial:false (only cfg-3120), and a narrower [12:04Z,13:59Z] query returns the same single entry, closing the earlier shard-2/3 enumeration gap; no revert or re-toggle exists through 13:59Z.

No deployment occurred after the 12:04Z config ramp through 13:59Z (all-services deployment query [12:04Z,13:59Z] count 0), and no order-service-side config change occurred in [12:00Z,13:59Z] (count 0).

The closest historical precedent is HIST-113 (2026-01-28, pricing-engine, 'quote timeouts'+'cpu 99%', capacity_saturation, match_score 4); no past incident describes a market-data-service serialization/schema-format regression.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately roll back config change cfg-3120: set flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct back from 100 to 5 on pricing-engine (the pre-incident value recorded at 12:04:00Z), then confirm pricing-engine cpu_pct returns to the ~40% baseline and latency_p99 to ~60ms.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change in the window and it immediately precedes the 12:05Z CPU/latency step; reverting it is the decisive recovery test and the mitigation. Revert is the experiment that the absence of any rollback so far has denied us.

recommended_actions.action: While the revert is applied, verify downstream recovery: confirm order-service error_rate falls from the ~8.1–8.4% plateau and the 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' errors stop, and that GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo WARNs cease.
recommended_actions.rationale: The observed failure chain runs pricing-engine saturation → 2500ms client timeouts → order-service error plateau; recovery must be confirmed at order-service, not just pricing-engine.

recommended_actions.action: Do not roll back or attribute the incident to market-data-service v5.2.0 (dep-6111); no action is warranted on it.
recommended_actions.rationale: market-data-service p99 (36.5–42.32ms) and error_rate (0.11–0.32%) are flat through its own 11:56Z deploy, and pricing-engine was at baseline for 8 minutes afterward — the protobuf change shows no measurable signal.

recommended_actions.action: Gate future GreeksV2 (and comparable Monte-Carlo) rollouts with a CPU/latency bake and automatic rollback: ramp in capped increments with an SLO gate on pricing-engine cpu_pct and latency_p99, and auto-revert if p99 exceeds the 2000ms quote budget.
recommended_actions.rationale: A single 5→100 ramp to 100% of traffic moved p99 from ~60ms to ~2535ms within one minute; staged gating with an automated budget-based rollback prevents this class of step change.

recommended_actions.action: Add per-request cost instrumentation and a pre-ramp cost estimate to GreeksV2: emit Monte-Carlo path-count/duration metrics (not only WARNs) and require review of expected CPU cost before ramping above a threshold share of traffic.
recommended_actions.rationale: The 6465–8361ms Monte-Carlo durations versus the 2000ms budget were the first visible signal and only appeared as WARN logs at 12:05:21Z; metrics would have surfaced the cost before the 100% ramp.

recommended_actions.action: Close the observability gaps that forced inference on this incident: add a pricing-engine replica/pod-count metric and ensure pricing-engine has a deployment object, so algorithmic cost can be separated from capacity loss without relying on proxies.
recommended_actions.rationale: replica_count returns not_found for pricing-engine, so the capacity-vs-cost separation was only indirect (flat request_rate, 0 restarts, flat memory).

recommended_actions.action: Fix the config-audit shard reliability (shard 2/3 down returned a partial, later-contradicted count-0 result) and alert on experiment/config ramps that change effective traffic coverage by a large factor.
recommended_actions.rationale: Incomplete config enumeration initially obscured the causal change and could hide a third-party change in a future incident; a 5→100 traffic-coverage ramp is a high-risk event deserving a guardrail.

recommended_actions.action: Establish an automated flag-ramp canary: hold each ramp at an intermediate percentage with an SLO-based auto-abort before reaching 100%.
recommended_actions.rationale: The step from 5% to 100% of traffic produced a step-function latency failure with no intermediate guard; a canary hold would have halted the ramp at the first CPU/latency breach.

data_gaps: The reported onset ('a few minutes before' the 12:16Z report) and market-data-service's deploy timing could not be reconciled with the causal-side onset using market-data-service telemetry: no log or 1-minute metric query was executed for market-data-service in 11:56–12:04Z, so a market-data-service-side log signal is not formally excluded. This does not weaken H1 (pricing-engine showed no signal for 8 minutes post-deploy) but leaves that specific gap open.
Blast radius is unmeasured: no other consumers of pricing-engine or market-data-service were checked, so it is unknown whether services beyond order-service were affected.

pricing-engine exposes no replica_count/pod-count metric and has no deployment object, so the CPU driver was confirmed only indirectly via flat request_rate, 0 restarts and flat memory — the algorithmic-cost vs. capacity-loss separation rests on proxies.

The pricing-engine protobuf/deserialization/schema-mismatch keyword grep was never executed (budget exhausted); the level>=WARN pull returned no such pattern, so absence is established only among WARN+ entries, not INFO/DEBUG.
order-service log query was truncated (30 of 225 entries) and ERROR-filtered, so an earlier WARN/INFO-level onset before 12:06:10Z cannot be excluded.

Full enumeration of config changes across every service in [12:00Z,13:59Z] relies on a re-run that returned partial:false with count 1, but earlier shard 2/3 failure means changes on ledger-db, exchange-gateway, redis-cache, kafka, portfolio-service or api-gateway are not formally excluded in every window variant.

No rollback or recovery of cfg-3120 was observed through 13:59Z, so there is no recovery-on-revert evidence — the single most decisive confirmation for a config-change root cause remains unobtained (this is a gap by impossibility, since no revert occurred, not an untested causal link).
what_would_change_the_conclusion: A pre-12:04Z onset: any elevated pricing-engine CPU, latency_p99 elevation, or GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo WARN before 12:04Z would break the smoking gun tying the incidence to the 12:04Z flag ramp.
Recovery without reverting cfg-3120, or continued saturation after reverting it — either would decouple the flag ramp from the CPU/latency step and point away from H1.
Evidence of a capacity loss rather than added cost: a drop in pricing-engine replica/pod count, a restart, or a request_rate change at onset would support capacity loss over algorithmic cost.

Direct telemetry showing market-data-service latency/error or a protobuf/deserialization/parse/schema-mismatch error in pricing-engine (including INFO/DEBUG level) at or before 12:04Z would revive H2.
A redis-cache hit-ratio collapse, eviction spike, or client/CPU step at or before 12:04Z would revive H3.
Discovery of a second config change or deployment on the failing path (e.g. in the previously-down config-audit shard 2/3) coincident with 12:04–12:05Z would introduce an alternative trigger.

It precedes the causal-side onset (pricing-engine CPU/latency step between 12:03 and 12:05, order-service first quote-timeout at 12:06:10Z) by ~8-10 minutes, not by the 'few minutes' implied in the report.

Independent per-service queries confirm NO deployments on the failing path services: pricing-engine deployments count=0 and order-service deployments count=0 in [11:00Z,13:59Z]. So no binary release to order-service or pricing-engine can explain the onset.

The only change inside the incident window on any service is a pricing-engine config flag: flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct ramped 5 -> 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic', author pm-experiments). The failing path does touch market-data-service: pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http) and pricing-engine -> redis-cache, while order-service's timeout signature is a 2500ms client-side request timeout, not connection refused or 5xx. So market-data-service is topologically on the failing path, but the observed anomaly (pricing-engine CPU pinned 98.6-99.3%, GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo paths=20000 taking 6465-8361ms) is internal compute, not serialization/parsing or a downstream connection error that a protobuf payload change would produce.
